Maladaptive Strategies.value: Situations or times of day that tend to bring on nightmares
I try to erase the memory of the event
I think about why the event has happened to me

Threat.value: I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building
Being superalert or watchful or on guard

Memory.value: I cannot put the memories of the event in the right order
I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind.
When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief

Negative Appraisals.value: My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed
I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened

issues.item: Triggers: Auditory (Explosion): Explosion or bang sounds
issues.explanation: For chronic physical abuse by a romantic partner, being triggered by male presence and related people is coherent, but explosion/bang sounds points toward combat, accidents, or blast-related trauma and is hard to reconcile as a core trigger here without any matching assault-context cue elsewhere in the profile.

issues.item: Threat: Risky Behavior: Taking too many risks or doing things that could cause you harm
issues.explanation: The rest of the profile reflects fear, avoidance, hypervigilance, fragmented memory, and negative self/world appraisals. Endorsing risky behavior pulls in the opposite direction and is not supported by other selected items; it reads as a different coping/symptom pattern than the otherwise strongly avoidant-threat profile.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Lost Community: I have lost my connection to my community and culture
issues.explanation: A marked loss of connection to community and culture is not well anchored to the rest of this intimate-partner-violence profile. The other appraisals center on danger, contamination, and shattered beliefs, but nothing else suggests cultural/community rupture, making this item feel clinically disconnected rather than tightly linked to the stated trauma formulation.

vignette: Eleanor Vance was seventy-two when the door slammed behind Arthur, the sound cutting through the living room like a blade. That specific evening, the physical blows had not been the worst of it; it was the sheer, unyielding presence of a man so close she could feel the heat of his anger, the rough grip of his hands on her wrists, the way his heavy footsteps echoed across the hardwood. When the heavy door shut, the sudden quiet felt heavier than the noise, and Eleanor had come to believe the world had fractured right there. She was an American social worker by trade, accustomed to holding space for others, but Arthur’s violence had left her convinced that the ground itself could give way. Now, at eighty, she still lives in the same quiet house, single and alone, yet the echoes of that evening refuse to settle. In the months that followed, Eleanor found herself waking at irregular hours, her sleep fractured by the simple act of drifting off and staying asleep. She grew wary of the late hours, the situations that tended to bring on nightmares, and would rise before the deep sleep could pull her under. She would lie rigid, trying to erase the memory of Arthur’s hands, convinced that if she kept the images at bay, they would lose their weight. Yet the memories did not line up in any clear sequence. Instead, they hovered around her as independent snapshots: a raised fist caught in the lamplight, a scuffed floorboard, the sharp intake of her own breath. Each picture carried its own weight, and when they surfaced, an overwhelming grief would rise in her chest. She spent years turning the event over in her mind, asking why it had happened to her, why she had stayed, why the world had allowed it. Her sleep grew lighter. She stayed alert to the creaks of the house, her shoulders perpetually drawn up. When she entered any room, her eyes moved automatically to the exits. She felt dirty, as though his anger had left a residue on her skin and in the air she breathed because of what happened. Her daily work at the community clinic soon became a quiet theatre of habit. In her office, a male colleague would sometimes bring files to her desk. When the heavy oak door clicked shut behind him, Eleanor’s breath would catch. She would find herself sitting just far enough from him to feel safe, watching the window, aware of every shift in his posture. The male presence felt immediate. When her sister or old colleagues visited, the familiar faces did not ease the tension; if they spoke too loudly or stood too close, Eleanor would retreat into silence. She was certain that people, no matter how well known, could not be trusted to hold her gently. The world, she had come to believe, was no longer a place of predictable kindness. Her beliefs about safety, about how relationships ought to function, had been completely shattered. None of these experiences dictated the others, but all lived alongside her. Now, at eighty, Eleanor sits in her therapist’s office, her hands folded tightly in her lap. Her PCL-5 score of sixty-six reflects a life lived on high alert, but the number only hints at the quiet exhaustion that has accumulated. She has come for help not because of one overwhelming symptom, but because the days have grown heavier with the weight of constant vigilance and the unrelenting pull of meaning-seeking. What she fears most now is losing the fragile stability she has built, that the world will once again close in around her, that a sudden door, a familiar face, or the mere presence of a man will unravel the careful boundaries she has maintained for decades. What she hopes for is simply to walk through rooms without scanning for escape, to let the memories settle without the grief rushing over her, and to rest, truly rest, without the quiet dread of what might happen next.
